{{Short description|Theorem in combinatorics}}
{{Distinguish|Dinitz-Garg-Goemans conjecture}}
In [[combinatorics]], the '''Dinitz theorem''', formerly known as the '''Dinitz conjecture''', is a statement about the extension of arrays to partial [[Latin squares]], proposed in 1979 by [[Jeff Dinitz]],{{r|ert}} and proved in 1994 by [[Fred Galvin]].{{r|g|z}}

==Statement==
The Dinitz theorem states that, given an <math>n \times n</math> square array, a set of <math>m</math> symbols with <math>m \ge n</math>, and for each cell of the array an <math>n</math>-element set drawn from the pool of <math>m</math> symbols, it is possible to label each cell with one of the elements of its set in such a way that no symbol is repeated within any row or any column. The resulting array is a partial [[Latin square]]: if all the cell sets happen to be the same set of <math>n</math> symbols, the labeling is an ordinary <math>n \times n</math> Latin square.{{r|c}}

==Formulation as list edge coloring==
The theorem is most naturally expressed in the language of [[list coloring]]. For a [[graph (discrete mathematics)|graph]] <math>G</math>, a ''list assignment'' <math>L</math> attaches to every edge <math>e</math> a set <math>L(e)</math> of permitted colors; a ''proper <math>L</math>-edge-coloring'' assigns to each edge a color from its own list so that adjacent edges (those sharing an endpoint) receive distinct colors. The [[list chromatic index]] <math>\chi'_\ell(G)</math> is the least integer <math>k</math> such that a proper <math>L</math>-edge-coloring exists for every list assignment with <math>|L(e)| \ge k</math> for all edges <math>e</math>. Since one may always take identical lists, <math>\chi'_\ell(G) \ge \chi'(G) \ge \Delta(G)</math>, where <math>\chi'</math> is the ordinary [[chromatic index]] and <math>\Delta</math> the maximum degree.

An <math>n \times n</math> Latin square corresponds to a proper edge coloring of the [[complete bipartite graph]] <math>K_{n,n}</math> with <math>n</math> colors: the two vertex classes are the rows and the columns, the edge joining row <math>i</math> to column <math>j</math> represents the cell <math>(i,j)</math>, and its color is the symbol placed in that cell. Under this correspondence, prescribing an <math>n</math>-element list for each cell is exactly prescribing an <math>n</math>-element list for each edge. The Dinitz theorem is therefore the statement that
:<math>\chi'_\ell(K_{n,n}) = n.</math>
Because <math>\Delta(K_{n,n}) = n</math>, this asserts that the list chromatic index of <math>K_{n,n}</math> attains its smallest possible value.{{r|c|z}}

==Galvin's theorem==
Galvin proved a considerably more general result: for every bipartite [[multigraph]] <math>G</math>,
:<math>\chi'_\ell(G) = \chi'(G).</math>
By [[Kőnig's theorem (graph theory)|Kőnig's edge-coloring theorem]] the chromatic index of a bipartite multigraph equals its maximum degree, so <math>\chi'_\ell(G) = \Delta(G)</math>. Taking <math>G = K_{n,n}</math> recovers the Dinitz theorem.{{r|g|bkw}}

===Proof via kernels===
Galvin's argument uses the notion of a [[Graph kernel|''kernel'']] of a directed graph. A kernel of a digraph <math>D</math> is a set <math>K</math> of vertices that is [[Independent set (graph theory)|independent]] (no arc joins two vertices of <math>K</math>) and ''absorbing'' (every vertex outside <math>K</math> has an arc directed into <math>K</math>). The proof combines this with the following lemma, the ''kernel method''.{{r|g|aigner}}

'''Kernel lemma.''' Let <math>D</math> be an orientation of a graph <math>G</math> such that every induced subdigraph of <math>D</math> has a kernel, and let <math>L</math> be a list assignment (on the vertices) with <math>|L(v)| \ge d^{+}_D(v) + 1</math> for every vertex <math>v</math>, where <math>d^{+}_D(v)</math> is the [[out-degree]] of <math>v</math>. Then <math>G</math> has a proper <math>L</math>-coloring.

The lemma is proved by induction: choose a color <math>c</math> appearing in some list, let <math>A</math> be the set of vertices whose lists contain <math>c</math>, take a kernel <math>K</math> of the subdigraph induced on <math>A</math>, color the vertices of <math>K</math> with <math>c</math>, and delete <math>K</math> from the graph together with <math>c</math> from all remaining lists. Every vertex of <math>A \setminus K</math> loses at least one out-neighbor, so the out-degree condition is preserved and induction applies.{{r|aigner}}

To apply this to <math>L(K_{n,n})</math>, whose vertices are the <math>n^2</math> cells <math>(i,j)</math>, fix a reference Latin square that assigns to cell <math>(i,j)</math> a symbol <math>\sigma(i,j) \in \{1,\dots,n\}</math>. Orient the line graph as follows: for two cells in the same row, direct the arc from the smaller reference symbol to the larger; for two cells in the same column, direct it from the larger to the smaller. Because the symbols in each row and each column form a permutation of <math>\{1,\dots,n\}</math>, the cell <math>(i,j)</math> with <math>\sigma(i,j)=s</math> has exactly <math>n-s</math> out-arcs within its row and <math>s-1</math> within its column, giving out-degree
:<math>d^{+}(i,j) = (n-s) + (s-1) = n-1</math>
for every cell. Lists of size <math>n = (n-1)+1</math> thus satisfy the hypothesis of the kernel lemma.

Finally, every induced subdigraph has a kernel: a set of cells corresponds to a bipartite graph between rows and columns, and interpreting the reference symbols as preference rankings turns a kernel into a [[stable marriage problem|stable matching]], which exists by the [[Gale–Shapley algorithm|Gale–Shapley theorem]]. Hence <math>K_{n,n}</math> is <math>n</math>-edge-choosable.{{r|g|galshap|aigner}}

==History==
Dinitz posed the problem in 1979, and it circulated for over a decade as one of the best-known open questions on list coloring.{{r|ert|c}} Partial results preceded Galvin's solution: [[Jeannette Janssen]] proved the statement for <math>(n-1) \times n</math> rectangular arrays, and for the square case with lists of size <math>n+1</math>, by applying the [[Combinatorial Nullstellensatz|polynomial method]] of [[Noga Alon|Alon]] and Tarsi.{{r|janssen}} Galvin settled the full conjecture in 1994 (published 1995) with the kernel argument above, which is elementary and self-contained.{{r|g}} Expository accounts were given by Zeilberger{{r|z}} and in the textbook literature.{{r|aigner|diestel}}

==Generalizations==
Galvin's proof extends verbatim from <math>K_{n,n}</math> to all bipartite multigraphs, and more generally to line-perfect graphs by way of Maffray's characterization of the line graphs possessing kernels.{{r|maffray}} [[Alexandr Kostochka]], Borodin, and Woodall strengthened the bipartite result by allowing shorter lists: for a bipartite graph <math>G</math>, a proper edge coloring exists whenever each edge <math>uv</math> is given a list of size at least <math>\max\{d_G(u), d_G(v)\}</math>.{{r|bkw}}

The [[List edge-coloring|list edge-coloring conjecture]] (or list coloring conjecture) asserts that <math>\chi'_\ell(G) = \chi'(G)</math> for ''every'' loopless multigraph, not just bipartite ones; it remains open in general. An even more general conjecture states that the [[list coloring|list chromatic number]] of every [[claw-free graph]] equals its [[chromatic number]].{{r|gm}} The Dinitz theorem is also related to [[Rota's basis conjecture]].{{r|c}}
